stops.name: Oberhausen: Das böse Quadrat, the Evil Square
stops.campa: With her Ruhr troupe she makes Das böse Quadrat, the Evil Square, a dance-play in which geometry itself is the demon. Bodies are pressed into the figure of the square and the square is wicked: repetition, right angles, the machine-form set loose among the living. The piece scandalizes and triumphs from 1924 onward and follows her for years, the first banner of what she will name abstract dance. In an age dancing its feelings, an eighteen-year-old sets a shape on stage and lets the shape do the willing.

stops.name: Hamborn, the second stage of the union
stops.campa: The troupe plays the circuit of the union: Hamborn, the mining city on the Rhine plain, its theater full of men with coal still under their fingernails and their families in Sunday cloth. Here the abstract dance is set before an audience that has never been told what dance must be, and therefore does not know to be offended. Skoronel counts these evenings among the proofs: the new form does not need the initiated. The body drilled to pure rhythm speaks to people who live by shift-whistles better than swans ever did.

stops.name: Gladbeck, the third stage, and the reckoning
stops.campa: At Gladbeck the third of the united stages receives her group, and the ledger receives its verdict. The Ruhr in 1925 is a land squeezed between occupation, inflation's scar and the pit-head; the municipal purse cannot carry an autonomous dance troupe, however famous its Evil Square. The engagement that made her a prodigy dissolves under her for money, not for art: the first lesson in the economics of the new dance, which she will spend the rest of her life outrunning. The troupe scatters; the choreographer packs her drawings.

stops.name: Darmstadt, ballet mistress at the Hessisches Landestheater
stops.campa: For the season of 1925-26 she goes south to Darmstadt as dance director of the Hessian state theater, a court house with columns, the opposite pole to the coal towns. Nineteen years old, she sets modern group work inside a repertory machine built for opera ballets, and learns how an institution resists a form. Darmstadt is brief and instructive: the theater will not be the vessel. What the abstract dance needs is its own house, its own school, its own bodies raised from the first exercise. Berlin is the answer forming.

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, co-direction of the Trümpy school
stops.campa: In 1926 she comes to Berlin and the fate closes its circuit: Berthe Trümpy, her elder from the Dresden studio, who has kept a school of her own in the capital since 1924, takes her as colleague and co-director. The house becomes the Schule Trümpy-Skoronel. The pact is exact: Trümpy gives money, order, administration; Skoronel gives the burning method. The celebrated soloist and the patrician organizer, two Swiss women in Wilmersdorf, set out to build the most modern dance school in Germany, and by every account they do.

stops.name: Berlin, the lesson of May 1926: the arms set free
stops.campa: An observer sits in her class in May 1926 and records a heresy: Skoronel trains the arms as an independent instrument, separate from the movement of the trunk, driving clear counter-rhythms through a single body: one pulse in the feet, another cutting across it in the hands. The chroniclers will say she is teaching, thirty years early, the polycentric isolations that jazz dance will one day claim for itself. In her studio it is simply the abstract method: the body not as a soul's gesture but as an orchestra of parts.

stops.name: Magdeburg, the first German Dancers' Congress: the breakthrough
stops.campa: In June 1927 the whole warring church of the German dance assembles at Magdeburg for the first Tänzerkongress: Laban's party, Wigman's party, the theater ballets, the critics. Into this synod steps Skoronel, twenty-one, and her solos carry the hall; the chronicle records it as her decisive breakthrough. With her group she gives Der gespaltene Mensch, the Split Man, Bruno Schönlank's speech-chorus made flesh, proletarian voices and abstract bodies in one machine. She leaves Magdeburg a name of the first rank, the youngest power at the council.

stops.name: Berlin, the Volksbühne: Der gespaltene Mensch and Erweckung der Massen
stops.campa: On the 21st of February 1928, at the Volksbühne on the Bülowplatz, the Split Man is given again in the Magdeburg casting, and beside it rises a new work of hers: Erweckung der Massen, the Awakening of the Masses. In the people's own theater the abstract dance and the workers' speech-chorus are joined: the drilled group as an image of the class waking into a single body. The canon keeps the pairing as her political sacrament: geometry placed at the service of the awakening multitude, form itself made comrade.

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, the new house: Blüthgenstraße 5
stops.campa: The school receives its temple. The architect Alfred Gellhorn raises for Trümpy and Skoronel a building of their own in Wilmersdorf at Blüthgenstraße 5 by the Westfälische Straße, dwelling and dance-hall in one, built 1927 and enlarged 1928, praised as the most modern house of its kind: a school constructed around the new body as deliberately as a laboratory around its instrument. Loheland's lesson is fulfilled: women building the house of their own discipline. The war will later erase the building; the canon keeps its address.

stops.name: Essen, the second Dancers' Congress, the woman in white
stops.campa: June 1928, Essen: the second Tänzerkongress, the great family portrait of the German dance. In the famous group photograph Skoronel stands luminous in an elegant white dress among the assembled masters, twenty-two and already a chapter of the history. To Essen too belongs her Trilogisches Tanzspiel, the three-part dance-play made with the composer Rosenberg and the designer Heinz Porep, which has its debut in this city: her largest architecture of the abstract group form, dance freed of story and of music's illustration alike, movement composed from movement.

stops.name: Berlin, Der moderne Tanz: the father prints the daughter's doctrine
stops.campa: Rudolf Lämmel publishes Der moderne Tanz, and at the book's heart stands his daughter: her treatise Der abstrakte Tanz fills its pages with eleven plates, and the libretto of the Tanzspiel is printed whole. The reform-pedagogue who once wrote to explain relativity now writes that she is the most significant dance-poet the Wigman school has produced. Father and daughter close the circle begun in the Zurich nursery: the theory of the fast body, set down in type. It is the fullest scripture of her doctrine that survives.
stops.quote: In the 'Quadrat' the abstract feeling was still conveyed in movement forms determined by the anatomical nature of the human body, so the new dance gives the dissolution of these forms into their dynamic linear components and the projection of movement curves into the plane of planimetric force elements.
stops.quote_source: Libretto of the Tanzspiel, printed in Rudolf Lämmel, Der moderne Tanz (Berlin, 1928); English rendering after Karl Toepfer, Empire of Ecstasy (1997)

stops.name: Berlin, the essay on Laban
stops.campa: In 1929 she publishes her essay on Laban, the pupil of thirteen now weighing the magus in print. Skoronel writes as she choreographs: exactly, structurally, without incense. The dance, she argues in these years, must become an objective, transmittable art governed by strict formal law: composition, not confession. Between rehearsals at the Blüthgenstraße she is building the theory of the abstract dance essay by essay, the only dancer of her generation whom the chroniclers call a dance-poet and a systematician in the same sentence.
